meta.blurb: Leila wins every argument and still feels empty. Over one summer at an old harbour boatyard, a retired boat builder teaches her to notice the proud, defensive voice inside her, and to hold it more lightly.
meta.bible: Leila Haddad: a clever, busy team leader of about thirty-four who always needs to be right. Mr Okafor: a retired boat builder with white hair and patient hands, who teaches without preaching. Dan: her colleague and rival. Priya: a young colleague, kind and quick with ideas. Sami: Leila's younger brother. Leila's mother visits once. The story takes place in one seaside town over one summer, from June to September. The old Boatyard on Harbour Lane has a small wooden boat that Mr Okafor repairs. Key terms: Ego means here the picture or image of oneself that feels it must be defended, not Freud's technical term, and the book says so. Lawyer is Leila's name for the defensive inner voice. Labels, Roles, Comparison, Envy, Pride, Humility, Awe, Curiosity, Credit. Many contemplative and philosophical traditions, including Buddhist, Christian, Sufi and Stoic teachers, speak in their own words about loosening self-importance; the book credits them in general terms and never ranks them. The science is hedged: some studies suggest awe and kind attention make people less self-focused, but results vary. Voice and tone: warm, practical, concrete, gently humorous; one clear idea in each beat; no claim that anything cures everything; Mr Okafor never preaches.

B1B2: Leila has just won an argument in a long meeting, and everyone in the room knows it. Yet on the walk home she feels strangely empty, as if she has won something that was never worth having.
In bed that night, Leila goes through the meeting again and again. She changes a word here and adds a clever answer there, although nobody is listening but herself.
The next morning, Dan thanks Priya in front of the whole team for a clever idea. Leila is sure that the idea started with her, and she feels her face grow hot.
On Saturday she walks down to the harbour to clear her head. There she meets Mr Okafor, an old boat builder, who is sanding the side of a small wooden boat.
Leila finds herself telling him the whole story, although she hardly knows him. When she has finished, he says nothing for a while, and then he asks who it was that felt so hurt.
Mr Okafor explains that everyone carries a picture of who they are. People often call it the ego, although psychologists use that word in other ways, and here it simply means the self-image.
A small child learns a name, a place in the family and what earns a smile. Slowly, from praise and from comparison with others, a picture of the self begins to grow.
Mr Okafor asks Leila to write down the words she uses to describe herself. She fills a whole page with labels, and the top three are clever, reliable and right.
Mr Okafor points out that a picture which feels fragile has to be guarded all day long. Every small insult becomes an attack, and every small success becomes a repair.
The self-image always wants to measure itself against other people. It either feels better than them or worse than them, but in both cases the attention stays on the self.
Comparison is like a ladder with no top. Whatever rung you reach, somebody is always standing one step above you, and that thought can spoil the whole climb.
Opinions can feel like parts of our own body. When someone disagrees, we feel attacked, so we fight to defend an idea as though it were an arm or a leg.
Mr Okafor gives her a task for the week. She does not have to change anything or fight the voice in her head, but only to notice what it says.
On the bus on Monday, Leila notices something she has never seen before. Without meaning to, she is judging the people around her by their shoes, their phones and their faces.
At her desk, Leila notices the story she tells about Dan: he is selfish, and he is against her. She realises that it is only a story, and a thought is not the same as a fact.
Mr Okafor suggests that she give the voice a name, which makes it easier to see. Leila calls it the Lawyer, because it always defends her and never looks for the truth.
The Lawyer always speaks for Leila and never speaks for anyone else. It collects every piece of evidence in her favour, but it does not ask whether the other person might have a point.
C1C2: Leila Haddad had won the argument, and everyone in the meeting room had seen her do it, with her figures neat and her voice calm and sure. Yet on the long walk home through the evening streets she felt strangely hollow, as though she had been handed a prize and then told it was made of paper. She could not have said why, and that puzzled her more than any defeat could have done.

At night she lay awake in the dark, playing the meeting again from the start like a film she had already seen a dozen times. She polished her best lines, added sharper replies to the things Dan had said, and cut out the moment when her voice had wobbled. It did not occur to her to ask who exactly she was performing for, since the only audience was the ceiling.

The next morning Dan stood at the front of the room and thanked Priya, warmly and publicly, for a clever idea that Leila was quite certain had been hers all along. Heat rose in her face, and a small, bitter voice in her head began to list everything she had done for the team that year. She smiled politely, but inside she was already keeping a careful and rather sulky account of who owed her what.

On Saturday morning she walked down to the harbour, hoping that the smell of salt and rope might clear her head. In the corner of the old Boatyard on Harbour Lane she found Mr Okafor, a retired boat builder with white hair and enormous patient hands, sanding the side of a small wooden boat. He glanced up, said good morning as though they had known each other for years, and went on working.

To her own surprise, Leila told the stranger the whole story, from the meeting to the sleepless night and the thanks that had gone to Priya. Mr Okafor listened without nodding or frowning, and when she finally ran out of words he let the silence sit for a moment. Then he asked, quite gently, who exactly it was that had felt so wounded.

Over two mugs of tea, Mr Okafor explained that everyone carries a kind of picture of who they are, made of labels, roles and opinions. Some people call this picture the Ego, although psychologists use the word in several other senses, and here it simply means the image of oneself that one feels must be protected. The picture is useful, he said, but it is only a picture, and a map is not the same thing as the land.

A small child learns first a name, then a place in the family, and then, very quickly, which behaviour earns a smile and which earns a frown. Little by little, through praise and blame and endless comparison with brothers, sisters and classmates, a picture of the self begins to grow, rather as a pearl forms around a speck of sand. Nobody plans it, and most of us never notice it happening.

Mr Okafor handed her a pencil and asked her to write down every word she used to describe herself, and she was astonished at how quickly the page filled. Clever, reliable, organised, fair, the one who gets things done, and, underlined twice, the one who is right. It was a flattering portrait, and for the first time she wondered whether she had painted it herself.

A picture that feels fragile must be guarded constantly, Mr Okafor said, rather like a cracked jug carried carefully across a crowded yard. Every careless remark becomes an attack that must be answered, and every success becomes a small repair that keeps the whole thing from falling apart. Leila recognised the tiring vigilance at once, for she had lived inside it for years.

The self-image, Mr Okafor said, is always measuring, and it can only arrive at one of two answers: that I am better than you, or that I am worse. The odd thing is that both answers keep the attention firmly fixed on me, whether the mood is pride or shame. Leila laughed out loud, because she could think of days when she had managed to feel both before lunch.

Comparison, Mr Okafor said, is a ladder with no top, because however high you climb there is always somebody a rung or two above you. Even the people who seem to have everything look up at someone else, and so the climb never produces the rest it promises. Leila thought of Dan, and Priya, and a school friend who had since become famous, and felt tired just counting them.

Opinions can feel like parts of the body, Mr Okafor observed, which is why a simple disagreement can feel like a blow. We defend an idea as fiercely as we would defend a hand, even when it is a trivial idea, such as the best way to plane a plank, and even when we are not very sure of it. Leila remembered how hard she had fought in the meeting over a point she did not care about.

Her first task, Mr Okafor said, was not to change anything at all. For one week she was simply to notice the voice in her head, as one might notice a radio playing in the next room, without arguing with it or trying to switch it off. She put a small notebook in her coat pocket, feeling oddly relieved that nothing more difficult was being asked.

On Monday morning, sitting on the crowded bus, Leila noticed something she had never seen so clearly before. Without any decision on her part, her mind was passing judgement on everyone nearby, on the man's tired shoes, the girl's loud music, and the woman who took up too much of the seat. She wrote three words in her notebook, and the third was embarrassment.

At her desk she caught herself composing the usual story about Dan, in which he was selfish, ambitious and secretly working against her. She stopped and looked at it, and saw that it was only a story, assembled out of two or three small events and a great deal of imagination. A thought can feel completely true and still be wrong, she wrote, and the sentence looked strange in her own handwriting.

Mr Okafor suggested that she give the voice a name, because something with a name is easier to see from a distance. After some thought Leila called it the Lawyer, since it argued her case from morning to night, and since it was never interested in what was actually true. It was a relief, she found, to say to herself that the Lawyer was talking again, rather than to believe every word.

The Lawyer, Leila discovered, had a very one-sided way of working. It gathered every scrap of evidence in her favour, ignored anything that pointed the other way, and never once wondered whether Dan or Priya might have a case of their own. Seeing this did not silence the Lawyer, but it did make her slightly less willing to accept its verdicts without question.
